sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
None. Every checklist line in this section is yes. One copy finding falls outside the checklist lines, and I'm passing it on for the director to weigh:

1. *(Copy, no checklist line.)* The times a passenger would plan around are vague. The first paragraph (about x 125–755, y 145–250) says the ferry runs "every forty minutes between early morning and late evening". The third paragraph (y 410–520) says "the last crossing leaves the quay before dusk". Readers act on these lines to catch a boat, and both can be read more than one way. "Early morning" could mean 6:00 or 8:00. "Before dusk" moves through the winter and could mean anywhere from 15:30 to 17:00. A passenger who reads it the late way misses the last boat and is left on the wrong bank. The page also sends readers to "printed timetables… in the shelter", so the times exist but aren't here. Fix: give the first and last departure from each landing, summer and winter, or link to the timetable. Defect. Weight: major if this page is where passengers plan a trip; minor if it only sits next to a timetable.

**What's working.**
- The page is clear in one sentence. The headline "Notes for ferry passengers" says who it's for and what kind of content follows, and the three paragraphs stay on that one subject: running times, bicycles, winter changes.
- Nothing on the page is extra. There are no boxes, rules or decoration, and one typeface with one dark ink sets a calm, practical tone that suits a passenger notice.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 8 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

First look: the eye lands on the bold title "Notes for ferry passengers" at the top left, then moves into three centred paragraphs of body text. It reads as an information page for ferry riders and feels plain and calm. Assumed job: give passengers practical facts about the timetable and bicycles.

Walk, What matters first:
- One element dominates: **yes**. The title, at about 40 px bold near-black (x≈120–593, y≈75–112), is far larger and heavier than anything else.
- Distinct text levels, no near-equal sizes: **yes**. There are two sizes, the title and about 19 px regular body text, with a big step between them.
- Headings also differ in weight, form or colour: **yes**. The title is bold and the body is regular.

No line came out `no` or `unsure`, so there are no entries to open.

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- The title (x≈120–593, y≈75–112) clearly leads. It is about twice the body size and much heavier, so the eye knows where to start and the page says right away what it is about and who it is for.
- The type scale has just two levels with a big step between them: a bold title and regular body text. No size is close to another, so nothing looks like a mistake. That suits short notes with no subsections.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does the visual weight balance, with no side, crowded or empty, that makes the page look about to tip? / Is the empty space gathered into a few deliberate areas? / Do the main divisions of the frame follow one proportion?** All the content sits in one column, about x 120–760, y 70–520, in the top-left of a 1280 × 800 frame. The right 520 px is blank from top to bottom, and so is the bottom ~280 px. The column is half the frame wide but starts 120 px in, so the frame splits arbitrarily into about 120 / 640 / 520. The page looks lopsided and half-built, as if a sidebar or image failed to load. That empty space doesn't frame the text: it reads as leftover. Arnheim (*Art and Visual Perception*, "Balance") says a heavy side needs a counterweight, and Tschichold (*The New Typography*) says negative space should be shaped on purpose, not left over. The fix has two options. If nothing else belongs here, centre the column in the frame, or give it equal margins, so the space becomes a frame. If the page is meant to be asymmetric, put something worth looking at in the right-hand area (the timetable, a landing map) so the empty space is clearly a choice. Before deciding, check that nothing failed to load on the right. Defect (reads as unfinished) plus convention. Weight: major. The words read fine either way, but the page looks broken.

2. **Is each centred or symmetric placement there for a reason the piece shows? / Is every element exactly aligned with an edge it shares with another, with no near-misses?** The three paragraphs (y 145–520) are centred, but the heading above them is flush left at x≈120. Prose this long has no reason to be centred, and the centring gives every body line a different start (x≈125, 129, 134, 149, 157…). The reader has to hunt for the start of each of the 12 lines, which slows down practical information that people scan for times and rules. Worse, the left ends of the lines hover a few pixels to the right of the heading's edge, with "Bicycles…" at x≈125 against the heading at 120. That looks like an alignment the page meant to make and missed, and the clash between a flush-left heading and centred body adds to the unfinished look. Tschichold (*The New Typography*) treats centring as a choice for a few short lines, and Müller-Brockmann (*Grid Systems*) says near-misses read as errors. Fix: set the body flush left on the heading's edge at x 120. Convention, with a real cost in reading speed. Weight: major.

**What's working.** The spacing groups the content well. The heading sits close to the first paragraph, and the gaps between paragraphs (~20 px beyond the line spacing) clearly separate the three topics (crossing times, bicycles, winter timetable) without breaking the column. Line spacing is consistent all the way down.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Whether the empty right-hand area is a slot for content that didn't load, such as an image, map, or sidebar, and how the column reflows on narrower screens. Check both in a live browser.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 8 yes, 5 no (exact alignment with no near-misses; empty space gathered on purpose; balance; centring for a reason; one proportion for the main divisions)

The text is clean except for one real problem: all three paragraphs are centred.

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Are paragraphs of several lines set flush left?** No. All three paragraphs (about x 125–755, y 145–520) are centred. Each is four lines long.
   - **What the viewer experiences:** every line starts at a different x, so after each line break the eye has to hunt for where the next one begins. That is a real cost on a page people scan for times and rules ("every forty minutes", "last crossing leaves the quay before dusk").
   - **Knock-on effects:**
     - Both edges are ragged, so the paragraphs read as a set of tapering shapes. Paragraph 2 ends in a short tail ("during the crossing.") and paragraph 3 in "changes for the coming week."
     - The heading sits flush left at x≈120, but the text under it has no left edge. Heading and body look like two separate items, not one article.
   - **Why:** Tschichold (*The New Typography*) and Bringhurst (*Elements*, 2.1.3) both hold that centring is for a few short lines, not for paragraphs.
   - **Fix:** set the paragraphs flush left on the heading's left edge (x≈120). Keep centring, if anywhere, for a short line or two.
   - Convention, with a defect's cost (slower reading and scanning of practical information). **Weight: major.** Centred text is the main thing that makes this page read worse than it should. Fixing it also fixes the rag and the missing left edge, so I filed those under this one line.

**What's working.**
- **Body type and measure:** the body is a plain sans at about 19 px, set at about 1.5 line spacing in dark grey on white. Lines run about 60–70 characters, inside the 45–75 range (Bringhurst). Once the text is flush left, this measure and leading will read comfortably; keep them.
- **Scale and spacing:** one family, two sizes. The bold heading is about twice the body size, which is a clear step. Paragraphs are separated by space alone, with no indent, which is the right single paragraph mark.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 29 yes, 1 no (paragraphs flush left)

Every line is yes, so step 5 is not needed.
